doi:10.1002/cam4.72371.abstract: Healthcare services and data ecosystems remain fragmented, inequitable and misaligned with patient, clinician and public health needs. Three pathways to patient-centred Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged to address this: data collaboration, Whole System Approaches and digital inclusion. Each has advanced the field. However, none delivers the continuous, participatory and outcome-grounded learning that equitable AI demands. The populations whose data drives AI learning must also be the populations who benefit from it. This principle has not been structurally embedded in any existing pathway. This narrative review defines a framework for operationalising Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) as a fourth, integrative pathway to patient-centred AI. AML is defined as continuous learning from real-world individual-level data to generate personalised, population-level insights returning direct benefit to the communities who produce them. A narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar (2018-2025) was conducted across five thematic domains: AI and machine learning in healthcare; real-world data and evidence; patient-centred care and digital health; data governance and AI regulation; and adaptive clinical trial design. Search terms covered healthcare AI applications and adaptive, continuously learning systems, emphasising prediction-oriented rather than static diagnostic approaches. Eligibility was determined through iterative thematic analysis. Eight systemic barriers to patient-centred AI are identified and the three existing pathways critically examined for limitations in addressing bias, validation and equitable implementation. AML is proposed as the mechanism that closes this gap, connecting systems medicine, personalised medicine and precision medicine through continuous, outcome-based learning, identifying three original conceptual contributions as enablers: Integrative Data Governance (IDG), Adaptive Clinical Trial (ACT) designs and Evidence Sandbox Facilities (ESFs). Progress requires globally standardised Healthcare Data Recycling frameworks, adaptive evaluation methodologies and ESFs enabling multi-stakeholder validation. Future research should address federated AML validation, collective consent mechanisms and alignment of regulatory frameworks with international AI governance standards.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70779.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, including esophageal (EC), gastric (GC), and colorectal cancer (CRC), impose a substantial global burden, with early detection remaining crucial for improving patient outcomes. The oral and gut microbiota are increasingly implicated in cancer development and hold promise as sources of non-invasive biomarkers. However, current evidence on microbiome-based diagnostics remains fragmented, and a systematic comparison of the diagnostic accuracy between oral and fecal sampling across multiple GI cancer types is lacking. To address this gap, a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus up to December 31, 2025, identified 43 case-control studies (59 cohorts) comprising 4452 cancer patients and 5809 controls. The pooled area under the curve (AUC) was 0.846 (95% CI: 0.824-0.867), though with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 86.5%). By cancer type, pooled AUCs were 0.746 for EC (5 cohorts), 0.886 for GC (8 cohorts), and 0.850 for CRC (46 cohorts). A bivariate analysis of 20 cohorts comparing sample types found no statistically significant difference in diagnostic performance between oral (sAUC = 0.863) and fecal sampling (sAUC = 0.820; p = 0.369). While these exploratory findings suggest that oral and fecal microbial biomarkers may offer comparable diagnostic accuracy for GI cancers, with oral sampling presenting a more practical option for screening, the results are preliminary. Significant heterogeneity, a limited number of oral cohorts, and the absence of clinical control groups highlight the need for large-scale prospective studies with direct comparisons and real-world validation to validate these biomarkers for clinical translation.

doi:10.1002/path.70127.abstract: Pretreatment prediction of neoadjuvant response remains an unresolved challenge in locally advanced rectal cancer, where management is moving towards risk-adapted and response-oriented treatment strategies. Prediction remains difficult because response reflects interacting tumour-intrinsic, immune, stromal, and spatial processes that are incompletely captured by standard clinical and radiological assessment. From a technology-centred perspective, in this Review we assess how molecular, spatial, image-based, and artificial intelligence-enabled approaches are being used to study and predict response to neoadjuvant treatment from pretreatment biopsies and how readily they may be translated into clinical workflows. Genomic profiling has its clearest current clinical role in identifying hypermutated immune-responsive subgroups, whereas broader genomic, epigenomic, and immune-repertoire markers remain largely investigational. Bulk transcriptomics has generated multiple response signatures with variable reproducibility but has consistently highlighted immune activation, interferon signalling, stromal remodelling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition as recurrent response-associated programmes; its most feasible clinical route is likely through targeted expression panels rather than open-ended transcriptome profiling. Higher-resolution approaches such as spatial transcriptomic and proteomic platforms refine these observations by localising signals to tumour, immune, and stromal compartments and capturing therapy-induced tissue reorganisation, but they are currently best positioned for deepening biological understanding and nominating rational treatment combinations for future testing. Established platforms such as digital pathology are closer to routine deployment as they build on clinically embedded workflows, although response-prediction algorithms still require robust external validation, calibration, and regulatory-grade implementation. Patient-derived models provide functional systems for testing candidate biomarkers and resistance mechanisms. Multimodal artificial intelligence may support response prediction by identifying complementary signals across data types and distilling complex signatures into parsimonious models suitable for clinical translation. Progress will depend on harmonised, longitudinal, multi-centre studies that couple biological depth with assay standardisation, model reduction, and prospective evidence that response predictors improve patient management. © 2026 The Author(s). doi:10.1002/path.70136.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with anaplastic features is a rare and highly aggressive subtype with an extremely poor prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying anaplastic transformation remain poorly understood. To characterize the anaplastic transformation molecular landscape, we analyzed genomic alterations in 5,997 conventional PDAC and 41 anaplastic carcinoma cases from the Memorial Sloan Kettering-Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (MSK-IMPACT) cohort. Additionally, four PDAC samples from the Kyorin cohort with both tubular and anaplastic components were subjected to spatial transcriptomics using the Visium platform. Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed to identify key molecular drivers. Genomic analysis revealed higher KRAS (90 versus 75%), TP53 (85 versus 60%), and CDKN2A (50 versus 30%) mutation frequencies, but notably fewer SMAD4 mutations (5 versus 20%; p = 0.022), in anaplastic carcinoma than in conventional PDAC. Spatial transcriptomics identified distinct molecular signatures, with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathways significantly enriched in anaplastic regions. Levels of ELF3, an epithelial transcription factor, were consistently downregulated in all anaplastic components. Importantly, we detected a strong inverse correlation between SMAD4 and ELF3 expression in both the bulk RNA sequencing cohort and spatial transcriptomic data. Functional validation using the KC-shSmad4 mouse model demonstrated that increased Smad4 suppressed Elf3 expression and promoted mesenchymal reprogramming. Our findings suggest a novel SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis that may contribute to anaplastic transformation in PDAC. The retention of SMAD4 functions coupled with ELF3 downregulation may promote EMT and contribute to tumor dedifferentiation. This SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis may provide a framework for identifying therapeutic vulnerabilities in this aggressive PDAC variant and further highlight the utility of spatial transcriptomics for understanding tumor heterogeneity. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05774-2.abstract: Outcome prediction in neuro-oncology remains challenging due to heterogeneity in tumor biology, imaging characteristics, treatment response, and patient-specific clinical factors. Although molecular databases have advanced understanding of brain tumor biology, many datasets lack broader data necessary for generalizable predictive modeling. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being explored to integrate these heterogeneous data sources and support precision neuro-oncology. A narrative review was performed using PubMed and Embase to identify studies evaluating oncology databases, ML models, multimodal data integration, and AI applications relevant to neuro-oncology. Studies published between 2020 and 2026 were preferentially reviewed, with additional landmark studies included when relevant. Traditional ML approaches including regression-based models, random forests, support vector machines, and gradient boosting algorithms have been applied to survival prediction, recurrence classification, treatment response estimation, and molecular biomarker prediction using clinical, imaging, molecular, and population-level datasets. More advanced architectures including natural language processing, large language models, vision transformers, geometric deep learning, and graph neural networks have expanded the ability to analyze unstructured and multimodal data sources including radiology reports, histopathology slides, MRI volumes, molecular datasets, and electronic health records. Multimodal AI systems integrating imaging, molecular, histopathologic, clinical, and socioeconomic data frequently demonstrated improved predictive performance compared with single-modality models. However, widespread clinical implementation remains limited by dataset heterogeneity, limited external validation, interpretability concerns, and inconsistent representation across patient populations. AI and ML approaches are increasingly capable of integrating complex neuro-oncology datasets in ways that more closely reflect real-world clinical decision-making. Although most current models remain investigational, multimodal AI frameworks may ultimately improve prognostic assessment, treatment stratification, and precision neuro-oncology care. Continued progress will require larger representative datasets, improved data harmonization, external validation, and clinically interpretable models.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05821-y.abstract: MGMT promoter methylation (MGMTpm) is a well-established molecular biomarker in neuro-oncology. We review current practices, challenges, and future directions for MGMTpm as a biomarker in central nervous system (CNS) tumors. The literature on MGMT function, and MGMTpm clinical significance and testing in CNS tumors was reviewed. We discuss the biological role of MGMT in DNA repair and the mechanisms by which MGMTpm leads to increased tumor sensitivity to alkylating agents. We summarize the clinical significance of MGMTpm in glioblastoma and its emerging relevance in other CNS tumors. Testing practices using methylation-specific PCR, pyrosequencing, and genome-wide methylation array-based approaches are discussed, along with challenges related to testing variability and "gray-zone" methylation, and emerging technologies such as nanopore sequencing. Despite ongoing technical and interpretative challenges, MGMTpm remains a robust and clinically valuable biomarker in neuro-oncology.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103252.abstract: The burden of second primary cancers (SPCs) is rising, partly because patients with a first cancer now survive longer. Two metrics coexist to quantify SPC risk: cumulative incidence, whose dependence on survival is well recognised, and the standardized incidence ratio (SIR), widely treated as survival-robust because it accounts for person-years at risk. Calendar-era SIR trends are increasingly reported and interpreted as real changes in risk, yet whether such trends could instead arise artefactually from concurrent gains in index-cancer survival has never been tested. We combined a calibrated simulation with an empirical analysis of SEER 17 (2000-2023). The simulation generated cohorts with strictly constant, stage-specific SPC risk, allowing only index-cancer 12-month survival to vary according to SEER-measured values, and applied a 12-month latency exclusion reproducing the SEER*Stat multiple-primary SIR procedure. Empirically, across 27 site × stage strata spanning wide survival-gain gradients, we related the observed 12-month survival gain (2004-09 vs 2015-18) to the calendar-year slope of the SPC SIR (Poisson regression), with six sensitivity analyses and a power calculation. At constant stage-specific risk, the simulated SIR drifted with survival, but across 200 Monte-Carlo replications the median bias-attributable slope was more than an order of magnitude smaller than the observed SIR slope (0.28 vs 7.9 × 10⁻³ per year), despite per-stage SIRs differing enough for the mechanism to act. Empirically, survival gain and SIR slope were unrelated (Pearson r = -0.00, p = 0.99), robust across all sensitivity analyses; power was adequate to detect r ≥ 0.50. Survivor-recomposition bias in the SPC SIR exists in principle but was small on average in the sites and calendar period studied. Unlike cumulative incidence, the SIR can generally be interpreted across calendar eras without major survival correction, although weak, site-specific, or longer-term effects cannot be excluded.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103253.abstract: Breast cancer treatment, commonly involving chemo- and/or radiotherapy, is associated with adverse cardiac effects, including cardiac dysfunction. While most research focuses on adverse effects during treatment, breast cancer survivors may also be at risk of developing cardiac dysfunction ≥ 5 years post-treatment. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of cardiac dysfunction in long-term female breast cancer survivors. CINAHL, Embase, and MEDLINE were systematically searched for articles that included breast cancer survivors treated with chemo- and/or radiotherapy and measured left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≥ 5 years post-diagnosis. The pooled prevalence of cardiac dysfunction, defined as LVEF ≤ 54% or a decline in LVEF of > 10% compared to baseline, was calculated and presented in a forest plot. Subgroup analyses based on treatment modality were performed, along with additional explorative forest plots to explore heterogeneity. Twenty-three studies encompassing 7309 patients were included with a median follow-up time since diagnosis of 5-30 years; Four studies included patients all treated with radiotherapy, of which two studies with radiotherapy as monotherapy and twenty studies included patients all treated with chemotherapy in combination with other therapies. Prevalence of cardiac dysfunction varied from 0% to 30%,. The pooled prevalence was estimated to be 10.8%, with significant heterogeneity (I² = 92.4%). Visual exploration of stratified analysis did not indicate explanations for this heterogeneity. Prevalence of cardiac dysfunction appears to be higher among long-term breast cancer survivors compared to the general population. Long-term breast cancer survivors remain at risk of cardiac dysfunction years after treatment, supporting the integration of cardiovascular risk assessment into survivorship care.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218861.abstract: Tumor drug resistance is still the core obstacle limiting the long-term benefit of modern anticancer therapy, especially in the context of treatment tolerance, persistence of minimal residual disease (MRD) and recurrence after treatment. Increasing evidence has shown that therapy-associated myeloid niches can involve cell recruitment, enrichment of pre-existing populations, or state reprogramming, together with local relationships among myeloid cells, tumor cells, stroma, vessels, and other immune cells. These niches can support residual tumor-cell survival, immune escape, local regrowth, and distant dissemination through overlapping mechanisms linking fibrotic exclusion and perivascular organization with hypoxic metabolic suppression and myeloid replenishment. The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, failure of antigen uptake and presentation, impaired T-cell priming, and phagocytic escape can further sustain treatment tolerance. Focusing on the myeloid cell state and common molecular circuits, this article presents an evidence assessment framework that interprets spatial and clinical associations alongside functional and pharmacologic findings without assigning hierarchical ranks. It summarizes lessons from clinical failure, considering potentially limited target contributions, compensatory pathways, inadequate exposure, and toxicity, while distinguishing drug exposure and local pharmacodynamic changes from clinical benefit. Candidate biomarkers, intervention windows, and selective delivery approaches require validation to guide mechanism-matched combinations. In the future, longitudinal tissue analyses, functional validation, and prospective studies should test whether these combinations provide durable benefit with acceptable safety in defined patient populations and treatment settings.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218889.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218890.abstract: Rising incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) and limited therapeutic options highlight the urgent need to define the drivers of its progression. The SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subset identified by single-cell transcriptomics is a functionally dominant population that extends beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm. Here, we dissected the molecular mechanisms by which SPP1+ TAMs reprogram tumor progression and determined whether the gut microbiota regulates this process in colorectal cancer. Using a multi-platform strategy integrating clinical specimens, murine models and CRC cell lines, we found that SPP1+ TAMs increase progressively during CRC evolution and exhibit crosstalk with malignant epithelial cells, and their abundance is associated with adverse clinical outcome. Integrative analysis reveals a significant positive correlation between SPP1 and ARG2 expression. Further, TAM-derived SPP1 engages CD44 on CRC cells to induce ARG2 expression. Mechanistically, ARG2 facilitates the interaction between USP10 and c-Myc to deubiquitinate and stabilize c-Myc, which transactivates the glycolytic enzyme HK2, driving Warburg metabolism that fuels CRC cell proliferation. Moreover, ARG2 secreted by CRC cells is internalized by TAMs, which reciprocally upregulates SPP1, creating a feed-forward loop that drives a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment. Notably, Bifidobacterium longum downregulates CD44 expression on tumor cells, thereby disrupting the SPP1-ARG2 axis and attenuating CRC progression. These findings identify the SPP1-ARG2 circuit as a therapeutic target and propose B. longum as a microbiome-derived precision adjuvant therapy for CRC suppression.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218891.abstract: Although neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) has improved survival in locally advanced gastric cancer (GC) and gastroesophageal junction cancer (GEJC), lymph node metastasis (LNM) patterns following NICT remain undefined. We aimed to characterize topographical LNM patterns after NICT and evaluate the association between lymphadenectomy extent, surgical approach, and survival outcomes. Data were pooled from 4 prospective clinical trials (NEOSUMMIT-01 - 04), comprising 126 patients with GC (n = 61) or GEJC (n = 65) undergoing curative gastrectomy following NICT. ypN0 was achieved in 71 patients (56%). In GEJC, station No. 3, 7 were high risk; No. 1, 2, 9, and 11 were intermediate risk; and No. 4, 5, 6, 8, 12 were low risk. In GC, station No. 12 was low-risk; D1 stations (No. 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) were high-risk, D1+ stations (No. 8, 9) and No. 11 were intermediate-risk. At a median follow-up of 36.2 months, 24-month EFS and OS rates were 76.4% and 90.5%. Nodal yield (≥ 30 vs. < 30) was not significantly associated with EFS (P = .611) or OS (P = .911). In exploratory comparisons within the GEJC cohort, EFS (P = .219) and OS (P = .290) did not differ significantly between proximal and total gastrectomy. In GEJC, distal perigastric lymph node stations (No. 4, 5, 6, and 12) exhibited low metastasis rates, while exploratory survival outcomes support prospective clinical trials of proximal gastrectomy in appropriately selected patients. Conversely, the broader residual nodal involvement in GC reinforces the continued role of standard D2 lymphadenectomy.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218893.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) drive the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), promoting oncogenic progression, metastasis and treatment resistance. While we previously established that intratumoral administration of poly(I:C) and R848 (TLR3 and TLR7/8 agonists) has strong therapeutic efficacy and triggers STAT1-mediated TAM reprogramming superior to monotherapies, this study evaluates the translational potential, systemic tolerability and immunological impact of their combined systemic (intravenous) delivery. Across diverse syngeneic murine models of solid tumors, including lung adenocarcinoma, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), fibrosarcoma and glioblastoma, systemic poly(I:C)+R848 administration significantly inhibited primary tumor growth and spontaneous lung metastasis. The treatment exhibited good tolerability under the conditions tested, with no body weight loss or histopathological damage to major organs. Treatment triggered a transient trend toward elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, CXCL10, CCL5), while anti-inflammatory markers (IL-10, IL-4) remained unchanged. In primary tumors, treatment-induced TAM reprogramming was evidenced by upregulated M1-like markers (Irf7, Ccl5) and decreased M2-like markers (Arg1), accompanied by enhanced Cd8 and Cd4 T cell markers and cytotoxic effectors (Prf-1 and Gzmb). Multispectral immunophenotyping confirmed this shift toward an antitumor macrophage phenotype, characterized by increased CD86 and decreased ARG1 across all primary tumors. Furthermore, treatment significantly prevented lung metastasis and tumor-induced splenomegaly, shifting splenic macrophages toward an elevated M1/M2 ratio in both fibrosarcoma and TNBC models. These findings demonstrate that intravenous administration of the poly(I:C)+R848 combination effectively reprograms TAMs, suppressing tumor progression and preventing metastasis across a variety of preclinical models of difficult-to-treat solid tumors.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.026.abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT) invades the central nervous system (CNS) via retrograde transport through motoneurons. Whether a host factor is needed to mediate TeNT trafficking has remained unknown. Here, using pull-down and mass spectrometry analysis, and by developing a luciferase-based in vivo transport assay, we identify receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPRS; PTPσ) as the retrograde transport receptor for TeNT. Global or motoneuron-specific PTPRS knockout (KO) abolishes TeNT entry into the CNS in mouse models. PTPRS-TeNT interactions occur in endosomes, prevent toxin translocation, and direct TeNT trafficking in neurons. Structural studies establish that the TeNT light chain and belt region bind to the immunoglobulin domain of PTPRS. Disrupting TeNT-PTPRS interactions blocks TeNT trafficking into the spinal cord; consistently, a PTPRS-binding-deficient TeNT mutant induces botulism-like flaccid paralysis. Thus, PTPRS is the host factor mediating TeNT trafficking into the CNS, revealing a targetable pathway for post-entry intervention and drug delivery into the CNS.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.028.abstract: Distal enhancers activate genes over vast genomic distances, but how this communication occurs and what signals are transmitted are poorly understood. Using real-time single-gene nanoscopy and targeted perturbations, we define physical parameters and mechanisms of enhancer-promoter communication. We find that productive interactions are dynamic, occur at a proximity of ≲100 nm, and are coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Enhancers and promoters find one another not only through passive diffusion; we often directly observe them being actively brought together by cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, which is a key determinant of transcriptional burst frequency. We also discover that specific general transcription factors (GTFs) of RNA polymerase II machinery are key to initiating transcriptional bursts, and enhancer-promoter interactions activate bursting by embedding the promoter within GTF clusters that form at the enhancers. Our results resolve the molecular and biochemical signals involved in long-range gene activation and elucidate the biophysical mechanisms for their transmission from the enhancer to the promoter.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103219.abstract: Pathological response (pR) has increasingly been used as a surrogate marker of neoadjuvant treatment efficacy in soft tissue sarcoma (STS), yet evidence linking it to improved survival remains inconsistent. This review evaluates the prognostic value of pR in neoadjuvant-treated STS. A systematic literature review identified clinical trials, observational studies, and retrospective studies assessing survival outcomes associated with pR, defined by residual viable tumour cells (RVT), necrosis, or fibrosis/hyalinization, in STS treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemoradiotherapy. Results were reported narratively given substantial heterogeneity between studies. Twenty-seven studies comprising 3961 patients (median 112, range 50-496) were included. Twenty-five reported RVT, eight necrosis, and seven fibrosis/hyalinization. Considerable variability was observed in the prognostic value of pR across studies. Low RVT predicted improved survival in 36% (9/25), high necrosis predicted decreased survival in 75% (6/8), and fibrosis/hyalinization was inconsistent (43% favourable, 29% unfavourable). Cut-off values, histological parameters and definitions, and patient and treatment characteristics varied widely. Analyses were predominantly unadjusted for confounders, including tumour grade, histological subtype, and resection margin. Current evidence is insufficient to support pR as a reliable prognostic predictor. The prognostic value of RVT, necrosis, and fibrosis/hyalinization varies substantially across studies, likely reflecting differences in histological subtype, tumour biology, treatment heterogeneity, and methodological inconsistencies in pR assessment. Standardisation of histological parameters assessed, their definitions, and pR categorisation criteria is required to determine the prognostic relevance of pR in STS. The proposed CHIRE framework provides a practical foundation for harmonising pR assessment and reporting in future STS studies.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106508.abstract: Although antigenemia is associated with poor outcomes in respiratory viral infections, the underlying mechanisms driving viral bloodstream dissemination remain not fully understood. Herein, we aimed to characterise SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N)-antigenemia kinetics in patients with severe COVID-19. We also sought to identify host and viral determinants associated with viral dissemination through a multiparametric integrated analysis and assess the associated risk of death. This observational study included hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 across three independent cohorts (discovery, n = 66; confirmation, n = 137; validation, n = 27), used respectively for identification, replication, and validation of findings, along with patients with mild COVID-19 and with severe influenza infection, as a disease severity and non-COVID-19 control group. From blood and nasal samples, N-antigenemia levels were analysed in relation to 45 host/viral parameters. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the association with in-hospital mortality. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to identify host determinants, and in vitro primary human airway epithelial models were used to assess epithelial barrier integrity and viral translocation. Across cohorts, we observed a significantly higher detection rate and concentration of N-antigenemia in patients with severe COVID-19 at admission compared to those with mild COVID-19 or controls (fold change [FC] >54.7, p < 0.001 [Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn post-hoc]). Type-I interferon (IFN-I) activity was the strongest correlate of N-antigenemia (ρ = 0.72, p.adj < 0.001 [Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg]), and longitudinal analyses revealed a strong positive sigmoidal relationship (p < 0.001 [approximate Wald test]). Patients with severe COVID-19 with neutralising autoantibodies against IFN-I lacked detectable N-antigenemia, further supporting a link between systemic viral dissemination and IFN-I activity. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed higher expression of interferon-stimulated genes in monocytes and dendritic cells in patients with a high N-antigenemia level. Furthermore, high N-antigenemia at hospital admission was independently associated with an increased risk of death (aOR 2.6, 95% CI 1.0-6.7; p = 0.042 [Wald test]). Finally, we demonstrated that prolonged IFN-I exposure in vitro appears to impair epithelial barrier integrity. These findings suggest that sustained IFN-I activity is associated with systemic viral dissemination and epithelial barrier dysfunction in patient with severe COVID-19. The concordance between clinical observations and in vitro data supports a potential link between prolonged IFN-I responses and these processes, although causality remains to be established. These results highlight the potential importance of the timing and duration of IFN-I immunity and warrant further investigation of its clinical relevance. doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108584.abstract: We conducted a randomized phase II trial to evaluate whether adding erlotinib to platinum/docetaxel improves clinical outcomes in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas, building on our previous single-arm phase II trial. This was a placebo-controlled, double-blind, single-center phase II study. Patients (N = 120) were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to receive platinum (carboplatin area under the curve 6 or cisplatin 75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) plus docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) with either erlotinib (150 mg/day orally until progression) or placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival, response rates, duration of response, and correlations of erlotinib-induced rash/biomarkers with outcomes. Median PFS was 6.1 months with erlotinib versus 4.4 months with placebo [hazard ratio (HR) 0.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.42-0.95, P = 0.026]. Median overall survival was 17.0 months in the erlotinib arm compared with 13.7 months in the control arm (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-1.04, P = 0.0718), meeting the prespecified type I error threshold. Subgroup analyses demonstrated numerically favorable PFS HRs across most clinical subgroups, with a more pronounced benefit observed in patients with oropharyngeal and human papillomavirus-related tumors. Development of grade ≥2 rash during the first cycle of erlotinib was associated with significantly improved overall survival (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.87, P = 0.021). The addition of erlotinib increased the incidence of grade 2-4 adverse events, particularly gastrointestinal toxicity, rash, fatigue, and dehydration but no unexpected safety signals were observed. The study met its primary endpoint, supporting the continued relevance of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibition in this disease. Although contemporary immunotherapy-based standards limit direct adoption of this regimen, these results provide clinically meaningful insight into EGFR biology and support further development of modernized, tyrosine kinase inhibitor-based EGFR strategies, including rational combinations and biomarker-driven approaches, to improve outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108596.abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are associated with poor outcomes, with many patients never receiving any cancer-directed treatment. Population-based registries from England, France, Italy and Spain share a similar picture: emergency presentation, rather than planned referral, accounts for roughly half of diagnoses, and >50% of patients with cholangiocarcinoma in England received neither surgery, systemic therapy nor stenting. This attrition is not exclusive to real-world settings: in PROOF-301 and FIGHT-302, a considerable proportion of eligible or randomly assigned patients never started their allocated treatment. BTC is also no longer a disease confined to older adults, with ∼7% of cases diagnosed in individuals <50 years of age. On top of this, access to reimbursed therapies, molecular profiling and expert multidisciplinary discussion remains markedly uneven across Europe. "Our patients deserve better" and closing these gaps in diagnosis, access to treatment and care delivery is as urgent as developing new drugs for this disease.

doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2026.09.005.abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy-free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone (n = 47) or 177Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT (n = 45). At a median follow-up of 31.9 mo, 177Lu-PNT2002 significantly improved PFS (median 17.6 vs 7.4 mo; hazard ratio [HR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.23-0.61; p < 0.001) and HT-FS (HR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.34-0.95; p = 0.03). Exploratory analyses demonstrated improved poly-PFS (HR 0.28, 95% CI = 0.08-1.03; p = 0.04), CRFS (HR 0.13, 95% CI = 0.02-1.10; p = 0.03), and CT-PFS (HR 0.46, 95% CI = 0.19-1.09; p = 0.07). No new safety signals were observed. With extended follow-up, neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before SBRT produced durable improvements in PFS and HT-FS. While poly-PFS, CRFS, and CT-PFS were exploratory end points, their improvement provides hypothesis-generating evidence that the addition of radioligand therapy to SBRT may alter disease trajectory beyond delaying PSMA PET/CT-detected recurrence.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.019.abstract: While accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy has increasingly been adopted in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy, there is a paucity of randomized prospective evidence guiding utilization. Given the marked heterogeneity in the presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, the American Radium Society (ARS) Thoracic Appropriate Use Criteria (AUC) Panel evaluated the appropriateness of accelerated hypofractionation in the context of multidisciplinary management. Five clinical variants representing manifestations of locally-advanced NSCLC were developed by the 15-member multidisciplinary ARS Thoracic AUC panel. The English-language medical literature was formally reviewed from 2010-2025 and scrutinized for prospective clinical trials utilizing accelerated hypofractionation for concurrent chemotherapy ineligible patients. All case variants were evaluated with respect to use of radiation technique, radiation fractionation, and utilization of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy with Modified Delphi methodology. Consensus recommendations were reviewed and approved by the ARS Executive Committee and subject to public comment. The literature review identified 228 articles, of which there were 14 prospective trials/registries including nine Phase I-II trials, four prospective registries, and one randomized Phase III trial. There was consensus that it is appropriate to utilize intensity modulated radiation therapy and proton therapy across presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, with the aim of constraining the lung V20Gy<30% and heart V40Gy<20% with accelerated hypofractionation. When utilizing 15-fraction accelerated hypofractionation for disease abutting the esophagus or brachial plexus, there was consensus that it is inappropriate to exceed doses of 45-55 Gy. With respect to PD-L1 immunotherapy, there was consensus that consolidative immunotherapy after definitive radiation therapy is appropriate, but that concurrent immunotherapy is inappropriate. There was panel consensus that it may be appropriate to utilize induction PD-L1 immunotherapy prior to radiation therapy in cases of bulky or N3 disease to test disease biology. Across variants, there was consensus that conventionally fractionated radiotherapy to 60 Gy in 30 fractions remains appropriate. The ARS Thoracic AUC Panel has provided consensus case-based guidelines on the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced NSCLC ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy reflecting the heterogeneity of disease presentation in this population. In absence of randomized prospective data demonstrating superiority of accelerated hypofractionation, conventionally fractionated radiotherapy remains an appropriate option.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.010.abstract: CD4+ tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are crucial for relapse in allergic skin conditions. However, the mechanisms underlying their maintenance and pathogenic potential remain poorly defined. Here, across multiple models of allergic dermatitis, we identified a C-X-C chemokine receptor 6 (CXCR6+) subpopulation within CD4+ TRM cells as a distinct pathogenic subset that rapidly induces relapse. This subset is supported by C-X-C chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16)-dependent interactions with CD301b+ conventional type 2 dendritic cells (cDC2s) for in situ maintenance. Functional blockade of the CXCL16-CXCR6 signaling pathway impaired proliferation and maintenance of CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells. In human atopic dermatitis (AD), CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells co-localized with CD301+ cDC2s in perivascular clusters even after successful anti-IL-13 therapy. These findings point to CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells as a pathogenic reservoir sustaining chronic and recurrent inflammation and suggest the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis as a therapeutic target to prevent relapse in allergic skin diseases.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103063.abstract: Cisplatin resistance remains a major obstacle in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet the contribution of the vascular microenvironment and its variation across HPV statuses remains unclear. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and bioinformatics analyses to characterize cisplatin resistance-associated cellular states in HNSCC. Cisplatin resistance scoring, pseudotime analysis, transcriptional regulatory network analysis, and cell-cell communication analysis were used to identify resistant subpopulations. Spatial localization, survival analysis, immune infiltration assessment, and drug sensitivity prediction were further performed to evaluate key candidate genes. Cisplatin resistance signals were preferentially enriched in tumor endothelial cells and were stronger in HPV-negative HNSCC. Endothelial cells with high resistance scores exhibited enhanced angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, hypoxia, and inflammatory programs. Multidimensional screening identified SERPINE1 as a key resistance-associated endothelial gene, showing significant upregulation and positive correlation with resistance scores. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses consistently demonstrated vascular-associated enrichment of SERPINE1, particularly in HPV-negative tumors. High SERPINE1 expression was associated with poor survival and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Drug sensitivity prediction suggested increased sensitivity of SERPINE1-high tumors to EGFR/SRC- and MAPK-pathway inhibitors, whereas no significant differences were observed for conventional cytotoxic agents. SERPINE1 defines a tumor endothelial state associated with cisplatin resistance in HNSCC and may contribute to HPV-related differences in the vascular microenvironment, providing a potential basis for therapeutic stratification.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103064.abstract: Renal cystic conditions are heterogeneous. We used a broad renal cyst-associated disease-gene framework to identify molecular programs shared with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), without modeling a specific cystic disorder or direct cyst-to-cancer progression. We identified 237 shared genes between renal cyst disease and ccRCC (TCGA-KIRC), performed functional enrichment, Mendelian randomization, and built a random survival forest (RSF) risk score benchmarked against published signatures and immunotherapy cohorts. Single-cell (Scissor, SCENIC, scTenifoldKnk virtual FOXM1 knockout) and spatial transcriptomics (RCTD, CellChat) were integrated with fibroblast subclustering and oncoPredict drug screening. Candidate FOXM1 inhibitors were prioritized by docking and 100-ns molecular dynamics, with isovitexin validated functionally. The shared program was enriched for epithelial development and ECM remodeling. Two direction-specific Mendelian randomization analyses supported associations between genetic liability to kidney cancer and related renal cystic phenotypes. The RSF score showed robust prognostic discrimination across cohorts and separated immunotherapy outcomes. High-risk tumors were enriched for Tregs, B cells, and fibroblasts. FOXM1+ malignant epithelium represented the high-risk state, with elevated CNV burden and regulon activity; virtual FOXM1 knockout identified COL6A1 and CD44 among 129 significant non-target perturbation hits. Convergent single-cell and spatial analyses nominated a COL6A1-CD44 communication axis associated with fibroblast remodeling, with F5_SFRP2+ fibroblasts as the most plausible receiving state. These fibroblasts showed ECM-remodeling, adverse prognosis, and pathway activation. Isovitexin emerged as a lead FOXM1-targeting compound, significantly suppressing ccRCC proliferation, migration, and invasion. These findings support a testable communication model involving FOXM1+ epithelium, COL6A1-CD44 and F5_SFRP2+ fibroblasts. The in vitro results also support further evaluation of isovitexin in ccRCC.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103078.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is molecularly, cellularly and spatially heterogeneous, and current staging systems and biomarkers incompletely explain prognosis and treatment response. This study integrated transcriptomics, machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and in vitro experiments to prioritize candidate CRC-associated markers and characterize their potential biological and clinical relevance. GSE44861 and GSE44076 from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and The Cancer Genome Atlas Colon Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-COAD) were used for differential expression, consensus differentially expressed gene (DEG) identification and functional enrichment analyses. Four machine-learning algorithms were applied for feature selection. Candidate genes were prioritized by differential expression, model importance and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance. GSE231559 single-cell data and spatial transcriptomics characterized the cellular source, pseudotime dynamics and spatial distribution of the core gene. TCGA-COAD assessed prognosis, pathways and computationally predicted drug sensitivity. Western blotting, Transwell and MTT assays were used for experimental validation, and public immunohistochemistry images from the Human Protein Atlas were used as supplementary protein-expression evidence. We identified 544 consensus DEGs enriched in leukocyte migration, chemotaxis, extracellular matrix organization, cytokine activity and metabolic pathways. Six genes were jointly selected: CLDN1, CDH3, KRT24, MMP7, NEBL and SCGN. CLDN1 was markedly upregulated and showed the highest tumour-versus-normal discrimination among the six candidates in the TCGA-COAD cohort. Single-cell and spatial analyses showed that CLDN1 was mainly expressed in CRC epithelial cells, displayed increasing expression across the inferred pseudotime ordering, and was enriched in malignant and mixed regions. In the TCGA-COAD cohort, high CLDN1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival and pathways involving the cell cycle, proteasome, autophagy, Hippo, ErbB and CRC. CLDN1 manipulation altered CRC-cell invasion and in vitro response to Nutlin-3a (-). These findings support CLDN1 as a candidate CRC-associated marker linked to malignant epithelial-cell states, tumour-associated spatial heterogeneity, invasive phenotype and Nutlin-3a (-) response. Further independent and prospective validation is required to determine its clinical diagnostic, prognostic and treatment-response relevance.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103111.abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) remains limited due to the inherently low tumor immunogenicity and the profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Herein, capitalizing on the metabolic traits and anatomical accessibility of CRC, we propose a broadly applicable oral strategy based on metabolically engineered bacteria (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for CRC immunotherapy. Mechanistically, cystathionine γ-lyase expressed by EHC disrupts redox homeostasis, triggering ferroptosis in CRC cells and thereby enhancing tumor immunogenicity. Concurrently, the intrinsic adjuvant activity of the bacteria amplifies the cancer-immunity cycle driven by immunogenic cell death and remodels the immunosuppressive TME. In vivo studies demonstrate that this orally delivered engineered bacterial platform not only suppresses the growth of orthotopic CRC tumors but also inhibits metastatic progression, indicating the induction of a potent systemic immune response. Immune profiling confirms robust systemic and gut mucosal immune activation following oral administration. Collectively, this oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform is precisely tailored to the features of CRC and offers a safe and effective immunotherapeutic strategy for this malignancy.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.005.abstract: As immunotherapy (IO) is increasingly utilized for treatment of endometrial cancer (EC) and cervical cancer (CC), optimal treatment strategies after IO remains poorly defined. We evaluated clinical outcomes, treatment patterns, toxicity, and survival among patients with recurrent EC and CC who received IO after prior IO. An Institutional Review Board approved, single-institution retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with recurrent EC or CC treated with subsequent IO between January 1, 2017, and January 1, 2025. Patients were included if they received at least one dose of IO after prior IO. Clinical characteristics, immune-related adverse events, response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Of fifty eligible patients, 36 had EC and 14 had CC. Pembrolizumab was the most common first IO agent in both cohorts. Second IO regimens differed by disease site, with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib most common in EC and pembrolizumab alone most common in CC. Following second IO exposure, objective response rate was 27.8% for EC and 14.3% for CC, while disease control rate was 55.6% and 64.3%, respectively. Median PFS with second IO exposure was 8.1 months in EC and 9.7 months in CC. Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events occurred in 20.0% during second IO. IO retreatment demonstrated clinical activity in selected patients with recurrent EC and CC after prior IO, with disease control achieved in more than half of patients. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and post-IO treatments.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04008-z.abstract: T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) is a key inhibitory receptor on cytotoxic lymphocytes, yet the mechanisms governing its context-dependent upregulation in tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we identify tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) signaling as an upstream driver of TIGIT expression. Integrated analyses of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed a consistent positive association between TNFα pathway activity and TIGIT expression across multiple cancer types, with strong concordance in melanoma and prognostic relevance in kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Mechanistically, TNFα directly induced TIGIT expression in natural killer cells via TNFR2 signaling, increasing chromatin accessibility at distal TIGIT enhancers and promoting NF-κB and AP-1 recruitment together with BRD4 and P300. Functionally, combined anti-TNFα and anti-TIGIT treatment suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival more effectively than either monotherapy in murine melanoma and colon cancer models. These findings define a TNFα-TNFR2-enhancer axis controlling TIGIT expression and provide a mechanistic rationale for dual TNFα and TIGIT targeting in inflamed tumors.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02786-2.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is an interstitial lung disease that advances over time and is ultimately life-threatening. Despite advances in antifibrotic therapies, disease progression remains largely unavoidable, highlighting the necessity for advancing mechanistic research and identifying new therapeutic options. Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2) is a key receptor for BMP signaling and exerts potent antifibrotic role in lung fibrosis; however, the molecular mechanisms regulating BMPR2 protein stability in fibrotic lungs remain poorly understood. In this study, we identify that the E3 ubiquitin ligase neural precursor cell expressed developmentally downregulated protein 4-like (Nedd4L) as a critical regulator of BMPR2 stability in lung fibroblasts. BMPR2 levels are markedly reduced in lung fibroblasts derived from patients with IPF and in lung tissues from experimental lung fibrosis models. Mechanically, elevated lipid peroxidation in fibrotic lungs induces K48-linked ubiquitination of BMPR2, leading to its degradation and attenuation of BMPs-induced Smad1/5 phosphorylation. Notably, Nedd4L overexpression counteracts lipid peroxidation-induced BMPR2 degradation and promotes BMPs/BMPR2 signaling by shifting BMPR2 ubiquitination toward a stabilizing K63-linked polyubiquitination in lung fibroblasts. We further show that Nedd4L is regulated through threonine phosphorylated by Raf1 kinase in response to increased lipid peroxidation. In vivo, fibroblast-Nedd4L-deficient mice exacerbates experimental lung fibrosis, which is significantly alleviated by BMPR2 overexpression. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecoganized regulatory mechanism of BMPR2 degradation in fibrotic lungs and indicate that stabilizing BMPR2 in lung fibroblasts may represent a promising approach for the treatment of lung fibrosis.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02840-z.abstract: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), constituting a major family of cell-surface transmembrane receptors, are essential for intracellular tyrosine phosphorylation and signal transduction. RTK signaling is crucial for cellular fate regulation and tissue homeostasis, and its disruption is linked to numerous diseases. Herein, we present a comprehensive review of signaling pathways involving RTKs, with a focus on their signal transduction mechanisms and key components, along with their interactions with major signaling cascades such as G protein-coupled receptors, Wnt, and transforming growth factor β pathways. We also elucidate the multidimensional roles of RTKs in cancer development and progression, highlighting their key effects on cancer stem cell maintenance, tumor microenvironment modulation, and other factors. Furthermore, we systematically summarize the roles of RTKs in noncancerous diseases, including cardiovascular disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, metabolic syndrome, autoimmune conditions, and fibrotic disorders. We then examine current RTK-targeted therapeutics, including small-molecule inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies, for the treatment of various cancers. Finally, novel therapeutic strategies, along with the challenges associated with their development and application, are discussed. In summary, this review will enhance the understanding of the mechanistic aspects of RTK signaling in major disease pathways and provide a detailed overview of recent advancements in targeted therapeutic interventions.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02905-z.abstract: Free radicals are highly reactive molecules that are ubiquitous in aerobic organisms. Among them, oxyradicals like superoxide (O2•-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and hydroxyl radical (OH•), collectively called reactive oxygen species (ROS), have drawn the most attention from researchers in the life sciences and biomedicine because these are the byproducts of aerobic metabolism that are responsible for the oxidative burden experienced by mammalian cells. However, it is now known this oxidative stress only occurs when cells are overwhelmed with ROS and that controlled bursts in free radical production orchestrate signaling pathways essential for organismal health. ROS like H2O2 is now a well-characterized second messenger that transmits signals through protein sulfur switches to activate cell stress coping strategies and induce pathways involved in proliferation, growth, and development. Additionally, defects in these redox systems have been found to be related to many diseases, which has led to the development of new therapeutic modalities to treat and prevent various disorders. In this Review, I will discuss the history of the Redox Biology and Medicine field and how these findings led to the discovery of the three known H2O2 signaling pathways that occur in cells; the floodgate, redox relay, and S-glutathionylation signaling mechanisms. Using this information and new findings generated with advanced molecular biology techniques that have quantified the cellular distance traveled by H2O2, I then propose that cells use these three redox signaling mechanisms to sense and transmit H2O2 signals over short and long cellular distances in mammalian cells.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02931-x.abstract: Pain is a multifaceted sensory and emotional experience that profoundly affects human health and quality of life. It functions as a double-edged sword: while acute pain serves as a protective warning signal, chronic pain compromises physiological and psychological well-being. Pain is now widely regarded as the "fifth vital sign," and given its rising prevalence and substantial global burden, chronic pain may also be considered a major chronic disease entity. Accordingly, elucidating the neural and molecular underpinnings of pain and developing effective analgesic strategies remain urgent priorities. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular and neural circuit mechanisms that govern pain. At the molecular level, ion channels, diverse receptor systems, and intricate signaling pathways play central roles in the transduction and modulation of nociceptive signals. At the circuit level, pain processing involves ascending pathways, descending modulatory systems, and distributed brain regions that collectively encode the sensory and affective dimensions of pain. Building on these mechanistic insights, we discuss current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions, as well as emerging approaches such as gene therapy, stem cell-based therapies and neuromodulation. Despite notable progress, several challenges remain, including the adverse effects associated with existing analgesics and an incomplete understanding of visceral pain mechanisms. Future research should prioritize the integration of multiomics approaches, advanced neural circuit mapping technologies, and artificial intelligence to refine mechanistic insights and enable the development of more precise and effective pain management strategies.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02952-6.abstract: Pulmonary nodules are highly prevalent in adult human populations, with a substantial proportion representing dormant cancerous lesions. We hypothesized that these pulmonary dormant cancers debilitate in growth owing to the lack of an angiogenic switch in tumors. In this study, we comprehensively investigated the hypothesis that specific pathological triggers can activate this angiogenic switch utilizing severe acute respiratory coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection-induced hypoxia as a primary physiological stimulus. Our findings provide compelling experimental evidence demonstrating that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces profound pulmonary hypoxia and severe tissue inflammation in animal models. This microenvironmental disruption markedly upregulates the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) within lung tissues. The resulting hyperactivation of the downstream VEGF-VEGFR2 signaling pathway effectively drives robust pulmonary neovascularization, a phenomenon frequently documented in clinical observations of COVID-19 patients. Furthermore, employing an established experimental tumor model, we demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 infection directly accelerates tumor outgrowth via this specific VEGF angiogenesis-dependent cascade. Crucially, the targeted administration of a neutralizing antibody to block VEGF significantly suppressed tumor progression and outgrowth in SARS-CoV-2-infected, tumor-bearing animals. Our data show that the COVID-19-induced hypoxia-VEGF-angiogenesis axis serves as one of the mechanisms for initiating tumor outgrowth in pulmonary tissues.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02964-2.abstract: Acne vulgaris is a widespread chronic inflammatory skin condition particularly affecting the pilosebaceous unit, with its pathogenesis intricately linked to excessive sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, overcolonization by Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes), and dysregulated host immune responses. Beyond its dermatological manifestations, the disorder is frequently associated with psychological comorbidities such as anxiety and depression, significantly impacting patients' quality of life. A genetic predisposition is evident, with associated polymorphisms involving pathways related to sebaceous gland activity, inflammatory regulation, and hormonal metabolism. Interactions among immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells, along with underlying molecular mechanisms, further contribute to its pathogenesis. Conventional acne treatments face challenges such as increasing antibiotic resistance and limited patient adherence. As a result, clinical research and practice are increasingly focusing on targeted, mechanism-based precision strategies. Recent advances in targeted biologics and vaccines directed against C. acnes have demonstrated promise in clinical studies, offering new avenues for acne management. This review provides a systematic overview of the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic classifications, and comorbidities associated with acne, with a particular focus on contemporary insights into its immunopathogenesis and molecular mechanisms. Additionally, it synthesizes current treatment modalities and explores emerging directions, such as acne vaccines and biologics, to serve as a reference for further mechanistic investigation and therapeutic advancement.

doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78580-z.abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

doi:10.1038/s41551-023-01017-1.abstract: Abstract Methods for the analysis of cell secretions at the single-cell level only provide semiquantitative endpoint readouts. Here we describe a microwell array for the real-time spatiotemporal monitoring of extracellular secretions from hundreds of single cells in parallel. The microwell array incorporates a gold substrate with arrays of nanometric holes functionalized with receptors for a specific analyte, and is illuminated with light spectrally overlapping with the device’s spectrum of extraordinary optical transmission. Spectral shifts in surface plasmon resonance resulting from analyte–receptor bindings around a secreting cell are recorded by a camera as variations in the intensity of the transmitted light while machine-learning-assisted cell tracking eliminates the influence of cell movements. We used the microwell array to characterize the antibody-secretion profiles of hybridoma cells and of a rare subset of antibody-secreting cells sorted from human donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells. High-throughput measurements of spatiotemporal secretory profiles at the single-cell level will aid the study of the physiological mechanisms governing protein secretion.

doi:10.1038/s41551-026-01812-6.abstract: Abstract Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking. Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. Each hospital contributed 50 radiographs for sequential model retraining without centralized data pooling. Continual learning achieved lower anatomical landmark localization error (0.67 cm versus 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for adult-only models) at 29 of 30 sites, with improved detection of deep intubations at 27 of 30 sites. These findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving collaborative learning can address critical gaps in paediatric AI deployment.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11250-8.abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93-5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

doi:10.1038/s41587-022-01307-0.abstract: Abstract Protein–ligand interactions are increasingly profiled at high throughput using affinity selection and massively parallel sequencing. However, these assays do not provide the biophysical parameters that most rigorously quantify molecular interactions. Here we describe a flexible machine learning method, called ProBound, that accurately defines sequence recognition in terms of equilibrium binding constants or kinetic rates. This is achieved using a multi-layered maximum-likelihood framework that models both the molecular interactions and the data generation process. We show that ProBound quantifies transcription factor (TF) behavior with models that predict binding affinity over a range exceeding that of previous resources; captures the impact of DNA modifications and conformational flexibility of multi-TF complexes; and infers specificity directly from in vivo data such as ChIP-seq without peak calling. When coupled with an assay called K D -seq, it determines the absolute affinity of protein–ligand interactions. We also apply ProBound to profile the kinetics of kinase–substrate interactions. ProBound opens new avenues for decoding biological networks and rationally engineering protein–ligand interactions.

doi:10.1038/s41587-022-01567-w.abstract: Abstract Monoclonal antibodies (Abs) that recognize major histocompatability complex (MHC)-presented tumor antigens in a manner similar to T cell receptors (TCRs) have great potential as cancer immunotherapeutics. However, isolation of ‘TCR-mimic’ (TCRm) Abs is laborious because Abs have not evolved the structurally nuanced peptide–MHC restriction of αβ-TCRs. Here, we present a strategy for rapid isolation of highly peptide-specific and ‘MHC-restricted’ Abs by re-engineering preselected Abs that engage peptide–MHC in a manner structurally similar to that of conventional αβ-TCRs. We created structure-based libraries focused on the peptide-interacting residues of TCRm Ab complementarity-determining region (CDR) loops, and rapidly generated MHC-restricted Abs to both mouse and human tumor antigens that specifically killed target cells when formatted as IgG, bispecific T cell engager (BiTE) and chimeric antigen receptor-T (CAR-T). Crystallographic analysis of one selected pMHC-restricted Ab revealed highly peptide-specific recognition, validating the engineering strategy. This approach can yield tumor antigen-specific antibodies in several weeks, potentially enabling rapid clinical translation.

doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02782-w.abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) contributes to cancer genome instability by enabling high-copy oncogene amplification and genetic intratumoral heterogeneity. Micronuclei (MNs) are common in chromosomally unstable cancers, yet their role in ecDNA-driven tumors remains unclear. Here we investigate how ecDNA damage, mitotic segregation and MN formation are linked. We find that ecDNAs are a major source of MNs following their damage, particularly under replication stress. Replication stress promotes mitotic ecDNA clustering, asymmetric inheritance, mis-segregation into MNs and reduced transcriptional output. Single-MN sequencing reveals that multiple distinct ecDNA species coalesce within individual MNs. Cells inheriting ecDNA+ MNs display impaired proliferative capacity and are more likely to undergo cell death. In patients with MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma, higher frequencies of ecDNA+ MNs at diagnosis are associated with improved overall survival. Together, these findings identify ecDNA mis-segregation as a mechanism that limits tumor fitness, highlighting mitotic ecDNA retention as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

doi:10.1038/s41590-026-02675-4.abstract: The regulatory mechanisms that maintain colonic immune homeostasis remain incompletely understood. Here we show that genetic deletion of Zbtb44, a previously uncharacterized member of the ZBTB transcription factor family, leads to spontaneous colitis and rectal prolapse. Zbtb44-/- T cells expressed increased IFN-γ, a pro-inflammatory cytokine strongly associated with human inflammatory bowel disease. Mechanistically, Zbtb44 undergoes SUMOylation, which facilitates its interaction with a conserved SUMO-interacting motif in T-bet, enabling binding to the IFN-γ promoter and enhancer to restrain chronic IFN-γ production. Together, these findings demonstrate that Zbtb44 is a key regulator of colonic inflammation, a role that could be exploited therapeutically.

doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04614-0.abstract: Menopause reshapes female physiology, yet current understanding is limited by small longitudinal cohorts that characterize it as a gradual transition. Large-scale biomedical datasets remain underutilized because the final menstrual period (FMP) age is rarely recorded. Here we present a computational framework, inspired by astronomy, that reconstructs FMP-anchored trajectories from cross-sectional data by removing the blurring caused by variation in FMP age across individuals. Applying this to two independent cohorts totaling 300 million laboratory tests revealed a step-like physiological cliff at the FMP including endocrine, skeletal, hepatic, renal and lipid systems. These discontinuities are absent in male individuals, are concordant across populations and appear markedly attenuated by menopausal hormone therapy. Dysregulation began more than a decade before FMP. These findings support a systemic, quantifiable view of menopause and provide a generalizable strategy for recovering hidden biological trajectories applicable to other transitions such as puberty or disease progression.

doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04689-9.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome with outsized impact on morbidity and mortality, yet its drivers and systemic consequences remain poorly defined. In this study, we repurposed longitudinal clinicogenomic data from 52,236 patients with cancer profiled by MSK-IMPACT (2010-2024) at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center to define episode-resolved trajectories of consensus-defined cachectic weight loss and linked these events to outcomes, serology and tumor genotypes. Cachectic episodes clustered near periods of disease progression and were associated with inferior outcomes in nearly all cancer types. Across diverse malignancies, cachectic weight loss episodes exhibited a consistent serologic signature characterized by lower albumin and hemoglobin and higher levels of liver enzymes. Numerous somatic tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutation across several diseases, were also associated with more frequent onset of cachectic episodes. Motivated by these observations, we developed a multivariate model to predict impending risk of cachectic weight loss in patients with lung, colorectal and prostate cancer, validated in an independent, external cohort from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (n = 5,785). Routine clinicogenomic data are, therefore, a scalable resource for discovery in cancer cachexia.

doi:10.1038/s41592-025-02797-x.abstract: Abstract Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are critical regulators of protein function, and their disruption is a key mechanism by which missense variants contribute to disease. Accurate PTM site prediction using deep learning can help identify PTM-altering variants, but progress has been limited by the lack of large, high-quality training datasets. Here, we introduce PTMAtlas, a curated compendium of 397,524 PTM sites generated through systematic reprocessing of 241 public mass-spectrometry datasets, and DeepMVP, a deep learning framework trained on PTMAtlas to predict PTM sites for phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, sumoylation, ubiquitination and N-glycosylation. DeepMVP substantially outperforms existing tools across all six PTM types. Its application to predicting PTM-altering missense variants shows strong concordance with experimental results, validated using literature-curated variants and cancer proteogenomic datasets. Together, PTMAtlas and DeepMVP provide a robust platform for PTM research and a scalable framework for assessing the functional consequences of coding variants through the lens of PTMs.

doi:10.1038/s43018-021-00292-8.abstract: Abstract Anti-PD-1 treatment has shown unprecedented clinical success in the treatment of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we performed temporal single-cell RNA and paired T-cell receptor sequencing on 47 tumor biopsies from 36 patients with NSCLC following PD-1-based therapies. We observed increased levels of precursor exhausted T (Texp) cells in responsive tumors after treatment, characterized by low expression of coinhibitory molecules and high expression of GZMK . By contrast, nonresponsive tumors failed to accumulate Texp cells. Our data suggested that Texp cells were unlikely to be derived from the reinvigoration of terminally exhausted cells; instead, they were accumulated by (1) local expansion and (2) replenishment by peripheral T cells with both new and pre-existing clonotypes, a phenomenon we named clonal revival. Our study provides insights into mechanisms underlying PD-1-based therapies, implicating clonal revival and expansion of Texp cells as steps to improve NSCLC treatment.

doi:10.1038/s43018-022-00356-3.abstract: Abstract Inferring single-cell compositions and their contributions to global gene expression changes from bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets is a major challenge in oncology. Here we develop Bayesian cell proportion reconstruction inferred using statistical marginalization (BayesPrism), a Bayesian method to predict cellular composition and gene expression in individual cell types from bulk RNA-seq, using patient-derived, scRNA-seq as prior information. We conduct integrative analyses in primary glioblastoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and skin cutaneous melanoma to correlate cell type composition with clinical outcomes across tumor types, and explore spatial heterogeneity in malignant and nonmalignant cell states. We refine current cancer subtypes using gene expression annotation after exclusion of confounding nonmalignant cells. Finally, we identify genes whose expression in malignant cells correlates with macrophage infiltration, T cells, fibroblasts and endothelial cells across multiple tumor types. Our work introduces a new lens to accurately infer cellular composition and expression in large cohorts of bulk RNA-seq data.
