doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0367.abstract: Despite advances in adoptive T cell therapy, therapeutic efficacy in solid tumors remains inconsistent, and the mechanistic determinants of treatment failure are incompletely understood. Increasing evidence suggests that effective antitumor responses depend not only on direct recognition of malignant cells but also on interactions with the tumor microenvironment, including non-malignant host cells that cross-present tumor antigens. Using an HLA-A2-transgenic syngeneic mouse cancer model that enables near-physiological presentation of human tumor antigens by both malignant and host cells, we investigated how TCR antigen sensitivity relates to therapeutic outcome. We compared T cell receptor-engineered (TCR-)T cells with different antigen sensitivities directed against the same HLA-A2-restricted melanoma antigen. Although high- and low-sensitivity TCR-T cells recognized tumor cells comparably in vitro, only high-sensitivity TCR-T cells mediated durable tumor regression in vivo. Improved tumor control correlated with enhanced recognition of cross-presented tumor antigen on tumor-associated CD11b+ myeloid cells and increased intratumoral effector activity. IFN-γ levels in tumor tissue and peripheral blood reflected intratumoral T cell activity and correlated with therapeutic response. Together, these findings identify host cell antigen recognition as a sensitivity-dependent functional correlate of TCR-T cell efficacy and provide a mechanistic explanation for the superior activity of higher-sensitivity TCRs in solid tumors.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0706.abstract: Concomitant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is a standard-of-care treatment for unresectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-SCCHN), but its immune effects, particularly relative to radiotherapy (RT) alone, remain incompletely understood. Using syngeneic murine models, we integrated Nr4a3-Tocky reporter analysis with single-cell transcriptomics and T cell receptor clonotyping to comprehensively profile intratumoural CD8⁺ T-cell responses following RT and CRT. We show that CRT uniquely drives robust clonal expansion of antigen-engaged CD8⁺ T-cells and biases differentiation toward progenitor-exhausted (TPEX) states, whereas RT favours terminal exhaustion (TEX). Single-cell analyses further reveal preferential clonal dominance within TPEX populations following CRT. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients treated with CRT, TEX populations predominated early after treatment, followed by delayed expansion of circulating TPEX-like populations at 3 months, suggesting phased recovery of progenitor-like T-cell states. Together, these findings demonstrate that CRT and RT induce distinct CD8⁺ T-cell differentiation trajectories and clonal architectures, providing insight into treatment-induced immune remodelling in LA-SCCHN.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0770.abstract: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major dose-limiting toxicity of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, yet the upstream mechanisms driving macrophage activation remain incompletely understood. Here, we established a xenograft model of human CAR T-cell therapy that recapitulates key features of CRS and combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with pharmacological intervention to define the inflammatory programs underlying CRS. CAR T-cell treatment induced dose-dependent systemic inflammation and remodeled the host myeloid compartment, leading to the accumulation of a distinct population of CRS-associated macrophages. Analysis of clinical scRNA-seq datasets from CAR T cell-treated glioblastoma patients confirmed enrichment of the CRS-associated macrophage gene signature following therapy in patients, supporting the clinical relevance of our findings. Transcriptomic analyses identified marked upregulation of the chemokine receptors CCR1 and CCR2 together with activation of CCL3- and CCL2-associated signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1 and CCR2 significantly reduced clinical CRS, inflammatory cytokine production, and macrophage activation while preserving CAR T-cell expansion, effector cytokine production, and in vivo antitumor efficacy. These findings identify CCR1/CCR2-dependent chemokine signaling as a critical regulator of macrophage-driven CRS and support chemokine receptor blockade as a promising strategy to improve the safety of CAR T-cell therapy without compromising therapeutic efficacy.

doi:10.1182/blood.2025030377.abstract: Phosphatase Mg2+/Mn2+ dependent 1D protein (PPM1D) is a serine threonine phosphatase known to regulate oncogenic pathways. PPM1D mutations are enriched in therapy-related MDS and AML, but the role of PPM1D in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) remains largely unexplored. By sequencing 519 MPN patients, we detected activating PPM1D mutations in 3.1% of them. Importantly, PPM1D was overexpressed in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in most PPM1D wild-type (WT) MPN cases. To elucidate the impact of PPM1D mutations on MPN HSPCs, we generated isogenic JAK2V617F+/PPM1D-WT and JAK2V617F+/PPM1D mutant (MUT) induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines from a MPN patient. Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) of iPSC derived HSPCs revealed altered TP53, DNA damage response and cell cycle regulation. scRNA-seq analysis of primary PPM1D-MUT MPN patient mononuclear cells (MNCs) further confirmed upregulation of MYC, mTORC1, OXPHOS, JAK/STAT, and NF-κB pathways and corresponding genes in HSCs. The allosteric PPM1D inhibitor (PPM1Di) GSK2830371 preferentially inhibited colony formation in myelofibrosis (MF) samples. Combination treatment of GSK2830371 with low dose inhibition of HDM2, a negative regulator of p53, significantly improved targeting of JAK2V617F+ HSPCs, while sparing normal HSPCs. Single-cell mutational and protein analysis of a clonally complex MF patient sample treated with this combination strategy revealed reduced mutated clones and increased WT clones by >4-fold. Dual PPM1D and HDM2 targeting also significantly decreased leukemic burden in a xenograft MPN model. These findings support PPM1D as a critical MPN HSPCs regulator and support dual PPM1D/HDM2 inhibition as a treatment strategy for MF patients.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026034288.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is limited not only by donor cell number and recipient conditioning, but also by loss of stem-cell fitness during collection and processing. Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells normally reside in a physiologically hypoxic marrow environment, yet routine ex vivo handling exposes them to ambient oxygen outside this niche. Although ambient oxygen exposure during ex vivo handling impairs hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) function, the metabolic basis for this effect remains incompletely defined. Using hypoxic handling as a physiologic reference, we examined whether functionally relevant consequences of ambient oxygen exposure remain modifiable in human CD34+ cells during ex vivo handling. Quantitative LC-MS profiling revealed that ambient oxygen exposure rapidly increased intracellular amino acids, including branched-chain amino acids, together with activation of nutrient-sensing pathways. This metabolic shift was associated with increased mTORC1 signaling, attenuation of lysosomal programs, and impaired primary and secondary engraftment. Complementary single-cell analyses supported a coordinated transition toward nutrient-activated states under ambient oxygen, whereas hypoxia preserved relative metabolic restraint. Transient restriction of essential amino acids or branched-chain amino acids during ex vivo handling restored lysosomal programs and improved engraftment of normoxia-handled human CD34+ cells. Pharmacologic LAT1 inhibition similarly improved engraftment. Together, these findings identify disruption of amino acid homeostasis as a previously underappreciated consequence of ambient oxygen exposure during routine ex vivo handling and demonstrate that a functionally relevant component of this injury remains modifiable after exposure to improve human HSPC engraftment.

doi:10.1200/po-25-01195.abstract: No curative options are available for medulloblastoma (MB) in the relapse setting. The tumor microenvironment (TME) influences progression and therapy response, presenting a promising target for therapeutic advances. Prior single-cell analyses have characterized the cellular components of the TME but lack spatial context. We hypothesize that spatial architecture, beyond cell composition, influences tumor progression and treatment outcomes. We performed spatial transcriptomic sequencing on 18 pediatric MB samples obtained at diagnosis, including two matched diagnosis-relapse pairs. Samples at diagnosis were stratified into high- and standard-risk groups. Spatial data were analyzed for spatial proximity to other cell types, cell-cell communication networks, and expression of cell cycle dormancy signatures. Findings were validated using immunohistochemistry in the same cohort. Our analyses revealed intertumoral and intratumoral heterogeneity within the TME, comprising tumor-associated astrocytes (TAAs), macrophages (TAMs), stromal components, and distinct subpopulations of MB cells at different stages of neuronal differentiation and cell cycle progression. We identified dense regions of quiescent progenitor-like MB cells enriched in patients with high-risk (HR) features and an increase in TAAs, TAMs, and dysregulated vascular endothelium following relapse. Our study presents novel insights into the spatial architecture and cellular landscape of the MB-TME, highlighting differential spatial patterns correlating with HR features. Future studies should evaluate their role in relapse and therapy resistance and may lead to uncovering novel therapeutic targets.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20711-3.abstract: Neoadjuvant therapy can improve the survival outcomes of patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer (BRPC). However, standard neoadjuvant regimens remain lacking. This study evaluated the clinical feasibility of tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel in the neoadjuvant setting for BRPC. In this prospective study, patients with BRPC preoperatively received three cycles of tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, and continued postoperatively. The primary endpoints were R0 resection rate and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). Exploratory objectives were resistance to this regimen. Of 30 enrolled patients, 80.0% (24/30) completed neoadjuvant therapy and underwent surgical resection. R0 resection was achieved in 80.0% (24/30) of the patients and in 100.00% (24/24) of those resected. The 12-month OS and RFS rates were 87.5% (95% CI 64.3-95.8%) and 82.8% (95% CI 60-95.8%), respectively, with median RFS of 28 months (95% CI 16.9-39.1). Most TRAEs were grade I-II, with no serious events. Quantitative proteomics combined with machine learning identified NT5DC2, FAM3D, CXCL5, and TMT1B as candidate biomarkers of resistance to this neoadjuvant regimen. In paired pre- and postoperative tissues from treatment-sensitive patients, CD8+ T-cell infiltration tended to increase and CD163+ M2-like macrophages were significantly upregulated after surgery. Neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel is promising for improving the resection rate in BRPC, with a favorable safety profile. NT5DC2, FAM3D, CXCL5, and TMT1B may serve as candidate biomarkers of preoperative drug resistance, and tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) analysis further reveals immune microenvironment remodeling in postoperative tumors from treatment-sensitive patients. These findings warrant validation in larger-scale studies. Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial registry (ChiCTR2200063680).

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20729-7.abstract: Data on robot-assisted minimally invasive esophagectomy (RAMIE) after neoadjuvant therapy, particularly after neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy, remain scarce. This study compares the perioperative outcomes of RAMIE versus conventional minimally invasive esophagectomy (MIE) in patients with resectable esophageal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy. We conducted a dual-center, retrospective study of consecutive patients with esophageal cancer who underwent MIE after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy or neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy between 2020 and 2025. Propensity score matching was applied based on preoperative variables. Perioperative outcomes were analyzed. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 137 patients were allocated to each group. The RAMIE group demonstrated a higher rate of left recurrent laryngeal nerve lymph node dissection (67.9% vs. 53.3%, p = 0.02) and yielded more lymph nodes in this station after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (mean 1.6 vs. 1.0, p = 0.02). However, RAMIE was associated with a higher overall incidence of postoperative complications (38.0% vs. 24.8%, p = 0.03). No significant differences were observed in operation time, pathological complete response rate, severe complications, length of stay, 30-day readmission, or 90-day mortality. In expert hands, RAMIE achieves perioperative safety comparable to that with MIE after neoadjuvant therapy and offers a superior ability to dissect critical lymph node stations. This technical advantage establishes RAMIE as a viable and promising surgical option, warranting further prospective investigation in randomized trials.
